books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Théodore Gentilz, “Fall of the Alamo,” about 1844

stimulus.source_note: Théodore Gentilz, “Fall of the Alamo,” about 1844. Public domain.
stimulus.text: A black-and-white painting of the Alamo mission compound in San Antonio, seen from above and at a distance. Mexican soldiers in formation fill the foreground and surround the low adobe walls, while more troops advance across the plain behind.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The battle shown in the painting most directly contributed to the Mexican-American War by doing which of the following?

options.text: Giving Texans a rallying cry, “Remember the Alamo!,” that kept the demand for annexation alive.
Persuading Mexico to recognize the independence of Texas in 1836, ending the dispute.
options.misconception: Mexico never recognized Texas independence; it treated Texas as a rebellious province until the war.

options.text: Causing the United States to annex Texas immediately in 1836, the year of the battle.
options.misconception: Annexation did not happen until 1845, nine years later, because the slavery question blocked it.

options.text: Ending all American settlement in Texas for the next decade.
options.misconception: American settlement in Texas continued and grew after the Alamo; the battle inspired more volunteers, not fewer.

rationales.A: The cry “Remember the Alamo!” carried the defeat into a cause, and the demand to annex Texas stayed alive until 1845.
rationales.B: Mexico refused to recognize Texas independence, which is one reason the annexation led to war.
rationales.C: The slavery question delayed annexation until 1845; the Alamo did not bring it about at once.
rationales.D: Volunteers kept coming to Texas after the Alamo, drawn by the fight rather than driven away by it.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the defeat. Every defender died, and on its face the Alamo was a loss.
2. Follow the cry it left behind. “Remember the Alamo!” turned a defeat into a reason to keep fighting for Texas.
3. Trace it forward. The demand for annexation survived nine years of delay, and annexation in 1845 led straight to war with Mexico.
Remember: a lost battle can win a cause — the Alamo mattered because its memory outlived its garrison.
